item.title: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Prediction markets are facing new limits on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would bar platforms from offering contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, an individual’s death, war, or U.S. military operations—the first legislation targeting the burgeoning industry to clear either chamber of Congress.

Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) introduced the bill, formally called the DEATH BETS Act, to prevent exchanges and clearinghouses overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from offering or processing those contracts. It would also ban contracts whose outcomes are reasonably expected to depend mainly on someone’s death, even if the wording does not mention death.

The bill passed the Senate by a voice vote and must still pass the House before heading to the president’s desk.

“They are offered with no regard for national security and in far too many cases, even basic morality,” Schiff said on the Senate floor. “These markets are operating in a Wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails.”

As platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown in prominence over the past two years, they have offered contracts on seemingly anything, drawing scrutiny over bets tied to war, violence, or human suffering. They have also raised concerns about insider trading, as users can trade without publicly revealing their identities, making it harder for outsiders to spot potential conflicts of interest.

Several cases have drawn politicians’ attention to these issues. One involved a Polymarket trader who made more than $400,000 betting on Nicolás Maduro’s removal from power before U.S. forces captured the Venezuelan leader in January. Kalshi also drew scrutiny over a market on whether Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei would leave office, which sparked a dispute after his killing when Kalshi declined to pay traders who had bet he would leave office, citing a rule that excluded death as a qualifying outcome.

In his speech, Schiff pointed to a Polymarket bet on whether NASA’s Artemis II mission would explode, raising concerns about wagers on astronauts’ lives. He also cited a bet on whether Russian forces would capture the Ukrainian city of Myrnohrad.

The companies’ leaders have previously pushed back on these criticisms. “We don’t list markets directly tied to death,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour wrote on X in February. Speaking at a conference in March, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called conflict-related markets a “complicated question” but defended their value as a source of useful information.

“Kalshi has never listed death markets,” a spokesperson for Kalshi told Fortune.

Polymarket declined to comment.

Other platforms, such as Novig, avoid these contracts altogether, limiting their offerings to sports markets and restricting trading to users 21 and older.

Pressure builds in Washington

The bill’s passage comes amid growing political scrutiny of prediction markets, particularly after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in this month’s midterm elections. Over the past week, several Democratic lawmakers have criticized the platforms on social media.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) pointed Wednesday to Kalshi’s decision to pause trading on contracts tied to President Donald Trump’s public remarks, which have drawn concerns about insider trading. “The CFTC needs to do more to stop insiders from cashing in,” she wrote on X.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) focused on younger users, calling Wednesday for an investigation and a ban on sports prediction markets. He criticized Kalshi for allowing 18-year-olds to bet on sports and said users under 21 had wagered $3.9 billion on the platform. “They call it a ‘prediction market.’ It’s gambling,” he wrote.

Though Democrats have been the most vocal, the scrutiny has crossed party lines. Besides cosponsoring the bill that passed Thursday, Curtis joined Warren last month in questioning Kalshi and Polymarket about potentially improper election-related trading. The Utah Republican has also backed separate legislation to ban sports and casino-style prediction contracts, citing concerns about young users’ exposure to gambling.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also announced plans to introduce legislation that would bar prediction market platforms from offering sports contracts without state or tribal approval, according to Bloomberg Law.

Update, Nov. 20, 2026: This article has been updated with a comment from Kalshi and Polymarket.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 16:53 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/senate-passes-first-ever-prediction-market-bill-as-democrats-turn-up-heat-on-upstart-industry/

item.title: Anthropic slid to just 5 cents above its IPO price, a stunning reversal of its first day pop
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Anthropic’s stock has come within a hair of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made one day earlier during the AI company’s blockbuster Wall Street debut.

Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.05 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading, before recovering some ground and climbing to roughly $87 in midday trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded.

At its lowest point on Friday, Anthropic’s stock traded just a nickel above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.

The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks.

Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day.

Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless of how the stock trades in the coming days and weeks.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 16:44 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/anthropic-stock-teeters-close-to-ipo-price-in-second-day-of-trading/

item.title: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain

Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates

For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.

So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.

"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."

This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.

After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.

From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.

"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.

Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.

Trump's meme coin

Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.

Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.

In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.

A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.

Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.

For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.

Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.

A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm

But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.

Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.

The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.

Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.

The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.

Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.

Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.

"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat.

But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.

World Liberty Financial declined to comment.

Another major deal for Trump's crypto venture

Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.

Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.

The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.

Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange — was pardoned by President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when the exchange got hacked earlier this month.

Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion, according to The New York Times.

While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits.

"Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment.

But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. Robert Garcia posted a social media message for the Trump family and his administration: "Lawyer up."

Source: NPR Business | Published: 2026-11-20 10:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/20/nx-s1-6038969/trump-crypto-profits-corruption-meme-coin-world-liberty-explainer

item.title: What impact has Brexit had on the UK and EU economies?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The UK and EU will hold the second summit since Brexit on Friday against a volatile economic backdrop.

Taking place in Brussels as the war in the Middle East hits the global economy, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.

Burnham has said that Brexit “has not worked”, citing damage to the UK economy from leaving the bloc. However, there are also economic challenges facing the EU. Here we spell out the economic context behind the talks.

How has the UK fared since Brexit?

After the 2016 Brexit vote, years of political turmoil and economic uncertainty damaged business investment. Trade has also been hit by new barriers and red tape for exporters under the Brexit deal agreed by Boris Johnson.

Analysis by the economist Nick Bloom shows that UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a 4% hit over a 15-year period.

UK services trade has fared better. UK goods exports to the EU in 2025 were 14% below 2019 in real terms. Exports outside the EU were 8% lower. Services exports were 28% higher to the EU and 26% higher elsewhere, fuelled by Britain’s dominant financial services sector, as well as travel, accountancy, law, professional services, telecommunications and IT.

Britain has conducted trade policy independently of Brussels since Brexit. This has helped and hindered the UK in different ways. The government has been able to cut tariffs on certain products to help households with rising living costs – including gherkins in last month’s budget. The UK also struck a tariff deal with Donald Trump on better terms than managed by the EU. However, critics say the UK lacks the clout it had as part of the EU to sign international deals, and that sharply diverging from EU policies is undesirable. This is because divergence could undermine trading relations with the UK’s single largest trade partner.

The UK has taken a greater lead in AI adoption than EU nations, ranking third in the Global AI Index. France is the highest-ranked EU nation, in sixth. This is in part – but not entirely – down to the UK taking a lighter-touch approach to regulation than Brussels.

So far this year the UK has grown at the second-fastest pace in the G7, as AI bolsters growth despite headwinds from the war in the Middle East.

How is the EU economy doing?

Brexit also had consequences for the EU, although as a larger market the changes have not been as profound. Barriers to trade have made Britain harder to access for EU exporters and migration has fallen.

Brexit gave a boost to populist political movements in EU countries. A wave of copycat exits did not materialise, with Britain’s political turmoil and economic uncertainty serving as a deterrent. But support for populist Eurosceptic parties remains, and battles over immigration, sovereignty and democratic accountability have not gone away.

The EU economy has faced similar global challenges to the UK – including from the 2022 Russian energy price shock and war in the Middle East. Trump has also aggressively targeted the EU in his tariff war.

Germany in particular has struggled from surging energy costs and Chinese competition hitting its industrial base. France has faced mounting political uncertainty, driving up borrowing costs and hitting growth.

Some EU economies have boomed – including former eastern bloc countries such as Poland, which has benefited from EU membership. Southern European economies at the heart of the 2010s eurozone debt crisis have also staged a marked turnaround.

The latest forecasts from the European Commission show that, as in Britain, the EU economy has proven more resilient than feared to the Middle East war. Germany has raised investment spending, particularly on defence, in response to Trump ripping up the western security consensus. AI-related investment has also bolstered activity.

What challenges lie ahead?

For the UK there will be infighting over the extent of ambition for the future EU relationship. This could fuel uncertainty for businesses and take up political and civil service bandwidth that could have been deployed elsewhere.

Rejoining the EU would not mean a return to 2016. Some UK involvement in EU supply chains may have gone permanently. Investors may remain nervous about British commitments to EU relations – particularly as the next general election draws near.

However, most experts are clear that there would be economic benefits from closer relations. Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that rejoining the single market could grow the UK economy by 2-5%, equivalent to £61bn to £152bn by the start of the next decade.

The focus at this UK-EU summit will be on a youth mobility scheme, a food and drink trade deal that could add up to £5.1bn a year to the UK economy, and an emissions linking agreement that could add £3.8bn a year.

The EU will face a series of critical elections next year, including in France, Poland and Italy. Populism is on the rise and Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls to become the next French president. Germany does not have elections until 2029 but the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party is gaining support.

Early next year there also will be a test for the EU with the appointment of a new president of the European Central Bank to replace Christine Lagarde. That will come against a backdrop of rising inflationary pressures, slowing economic growth and pressures on government borrowing costs. The Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos is considered the frontrunner.

Britain is also expected to face a tougher year in 2027 due to the impact of high inflation from the war in the Middle East, with the squeeze on households also expected to weigh on growth.

Source: The Guardian Business | Published: 2026-11-20 07:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/20/what-impact-brexit-uk-eu-economies
